title: WTP Research and A/B Pricing Experiments
description: Master willingness-to-pay research methods and design rigorous A/B pricing experiments to optimize revenue.

interactions.prompt: Which method best addresses the hypothetical bias problem in WTP research?

options.text: Directly asking customers what they'd pay
Incentive-compatible experiments with real purchase decisions
Focus groups discussing perceived value
Surveying competitors' published pricing pages

interactions.teachingPreamble: Willingness-to-pay (WTP) research suffers from hypothetical bias—customers overstate what they'd pay when no real money is at stake. Becker-DeGroot-Marschak (BDM) auctions and real purchase experiments solve this by making responses consequential. Slack used incentive-compatible conjoint studies before launching paid tiers, finding WTP was 22% lower than direct survey responses suggested.

interactions.prompt: A SaaS company ran a Van Westendorp survey (n=2,400). Results: Point of Marginal Cheapness = $29, Indifference Price = $49, Point of Marginal Expensiveness = $69, Optimal Price Point = $42. Current price is $55. What's the key insight?

options.text: Price is above the optimal range; expect conversion drag
Price is perfectly centered in the acceptable range
The $29 floor suggests dropping price immediately
Van Westendorp is unreliable at this sample size

interactions.prompt: Why is randomizing A/B pricing tests at the user level often problematic for B2B SaaS?

options.text: Users within one company may see different prices, eroding trust
User-level randomization always produces smaller sample sizes
It violates GDPR regulations in all jurisdictions
Pricing experiments only work with physical products

interactions.teachingPreamble: A/B pricing experiments require careful unit-of-randomization design. HubSpot learned this when colleagues at the same company saw different prices during a test, generating support tickets and social media backlash. Best practice for B2B is account-level or cohort-level randomization, and for B2C, geographic or time-based splits reduce contamination risk while maintaining statistical power.

interactions.prompt: In A/B pricing experiments, the minimum detectable effect (MDE) determines sample size: detecting a ____% revenue lift typically requires 4x the sample needed to detect a 10% lift.

You're optimizing pricing for a fintech app with 80K MAU. You can run a live A/B price test (fast, real data, but risk of customer backlash) or a conjoint study with 1,500 prospects (slower, no backlash, but hypothetical bias). Which do you choose?

options.text: Live A/B test—real purchase data outweighs backlash risk
Conjoint study—fintech trust is fragile, avoid perception damage
Run both simultaneously to triangulate results
Skip research and match competitor pricing instead

interactions.prompt: Booking.com tested showing a crossed-out "$189" next to the actual "$129" price. Conversion rose 14%. What secondary metric must you monitor to validate this tactic long-term?

options.text: Cancellation and refund rates as a proxy for buyer's remorse
Total page views on the listing
Number of new user sign-ups per day
Average session duration on the checkout page

interactions.teachingPreamble: Anchoring in price optimization goes beyond simple high-low framing. Sophisticated operators use reference price anchoring (showing original vs. discounted price) and decoy anchoring (adding an unattractive option to steer choice). However, aggressive anchoring can inflate short-term conversion while increasing post-purchase regret. Booking.com and Amazon continuously monitor downstream metrics like cancellation rates and return rates to ensure anchoring lifts net revenue, not just gross bookings.

interactions.prompt: You're launching a new enterprise analytics tier. Rank these price optimization steps from first to last: (a) Run a live A/B test on the shortlisted prices, (b) Conduct conjoint analysis to map WTP across segments, (c) Analyze post-launch cohort retention by price point, (d) Define customer segments and value metrics.

options.text: Run a live A/B test on shortlisted prices
Conduct conjoint analysis to map WTP across segments
Analyze post-launch cohort retention by price point
Define customer segments and value metrics

interactions.prompt: Your A/B pricing test showed the higher price ($79) outperformed ($59) on revenue per user by 18%. But a journalist just tweeted screenshots showing two prices to 45K followers, calling it discriminatory. What's your best immediate move?

options.text: End the test, honor the lower price for all, publish a transparency blog
Ignore it—A/B testing is standard practice and will blow over
Immediately raise everyone to $79 since it won the test
Delete the tweet by contacting the journalist privately

interactions.priorContext: You had been running a successful A/B pricing experiment with strong statistical results favoring the higher price. Now a public relations crisis has emerged that changes the decision calculus from pure optimization to brand trust management.
